title: Conditional Statements, Converses and Counterexamples
seo_title: Geometry Conditional Statements and Counterexamples Worksheets (TEKS G.4B)
standard_text: G.4B identify and determine the validity of the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of a conditional statement and recognize the connection between a biconditional statement and a true conditional statement with a true converse; G.4C verify that a conjecture is false using a counterexample
meta_desc: Free Geometry worksheets for Texas TEKS G.4B and G.4C: conditional statements, converse, inverse, contrapositive, biconditionals and counterexamples. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A conditional and its contrapositive have the same truth value.
key_sub: One counterexample proves a statement false.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A conditional: if p, then q. p is the hypothesis, q the conclusion.
  • Converse: if q, then p. Inverse: if not p, then not q. Contrapositive: if not q, then not p.
  • A conditional and its contrapositive are always both true or both false.
  • A biconditional (p if and only if q) is true when the conditional and its converse are both true.
  • One counterexample shows a statement is false.

Examples

Example

If an angle is 30°, then it is acute.

converse: if an angle is acute, it is 30°

Answer: converse false (60° is acute)

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Swapping inverse and converseConverse swaps; inverse negates.
Assuming the converse is trueCheck it separately.
Giving an example instead of a counterexampleIt must make the hypothesis true and the conclusion false.

items.q: What is the hypothesis of this statement? If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary.

items.q: Which is a counterexample to this statement? If a polygon has four sides, then it is a rectangle.
items.e: A counterexample makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false. A trapezoid has four sides but is not a rectangle. (A triangle does not have four sides, so it does not test the statement.) A trapezoid.

items.q: Which is a counterexample to this statement? If two angles are supplementary, then they form a linear pair.
c: Two angles of 90° and 90° on a line
Two adjacent angles of 120° and 60° on a line

items.e: A counterexample makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false. 1 > −2, but 1² = 1 is not greater than (−2)² = 4. x = 1, y = −2.

items.q: Given: If Owen gets an A on the test, then he gets an A in the class. “Owen gets an A on the test” is true. What can you conclude?
c: If he gets an A in the class, then Owen gets an A on the test.
He gets an A in the class.
items.e: Law of Detachment: the hypothesis is true, so the conclusion is true. He gets an A in the class.

items.q: Given: If the temperature drops below 32°F, then the pond freezes, and If the pond freezes, then people can skate on the pond. What can you conclude by the Law of Syllogism?
c: If people can skate on the pond, then the temperature drops below 32°F.
If the temperature drops below 32°F, then people can skate on the pond.
If the pond freezes, then the temperature drops below 32°F.
items.e: The conclusion of the first statement is the hypothesis of the second, so chain them: If the temperature drops below 32°F, then people can skate on the pond.

items.q: Which property justifies this step? If 4x = 36, then x = 9.
items.e: Both sides were divided by 4. Division Property of Equality.

items.q: Which property justifies this step? If 4(x + 4) = 52, then 4x + 16 = 52.
items.e: 4 was multiplied by each term inside the parentheses. Distributive Property.

items.q: Which property justifies this step? If x − 3 = 20, then x = 23.
items.e: 3 was added to both sides. Addition Property of Equality.
